chapter.title: Fetching a page and keeping a copy

cards.body: A web page is not a page. It is one long string of text, and your agent can read it the way your clipping clerk reads the morning paper: today the clerk buys the paper, cuts nothing, and files the whole thing with the date written on top. **Without that dated copy, tomorrow there is nothing to compare.**

cards.prompt: Your clipping clerk reads rival Lantern Payroll's pricing page on Monday, nods, and bins the paper. On Tuesday you ask what changed. What can the clerk honestly say?

options.text: Prices went up, I remember it clearly
Nothing to compare against: Monday's copy is gone
Tuesday's page is the only one that matters

whyNot.a: That's memory, not a copy: memory is exactly what the agent does not have between runs.
whyNot.c: That's reading, not tracking: one copy tells you what a page says, never what changed.

cards.reteach: A change is a difference between two things. If you keep only today, you have one thing. Yesterday's saved copy is the second thing, and the whole reason to save.

cards.title: Buying the paper
cards.body:
When your browser shows a page, it first *downloads* it: it asks the website's computer for the page and gets text back. Your agent can make the same request with one line of code and get the same text, no browser needed. That text is *HTML*, the page's raw form, full of tags like

and

that tell a browser where things go. A pricing page that reads as 300 words on screen can arrive as 5,000 lines of HTML. **Fetch means download the raw text, then strip the tags** so you keep only the words a person would see. That is the paper, delivered.

cards.title: Priya's first clipping
cards.body: Priya tracks a payroll rival called Lantern. She points her agent at Lantern's pricing page. The raw download is 212 KB of HTML, and the word 'price' appears 41 times, mostly inside menu code. After stripping tags she has 640 words, 3 plan names and 3 numbers. She saves it as lantern-pricing-2026-10-04.txt, opens it, reads the plans. The file is boring. That is the point: boring today, evidence tomorrow, because **now she owns a copy of Lantern's Monday**.

cards.prompt: Priya's agent saves Lantern's pricing page each morning. Which filename keeps a copy she can compare against next week?

options.text: lantern-pricing-2026-10-04.txt, a new file each day

whyNot.a: That's today replacing yesterday: the moment it overwrites, the comparison is gone.
whyNot.c: That's the paper before stripping, with no date: raw tags clutter the compare, and 'latest' is still only one sheet.

cards.reteach: The date in the filename turns one file into a stack. Each day adds a layer; next week you pull out two and hold them side by side. Overwrite, and the stack is always one sheet thick.

cards.title: When the paper comes blank
cards.body:
Mostly a page is text your agent can read. The exceptions matter. Some pages arrive almost empty, with a line like 'Please enable JavaScript', because the real words are added later by code running inside a browser. Your agent has no browser, so it gets the empty shell.

Other sites spot a robot and send an 'Access denied' page, or a *403*, the web's number for 'no'. Both look like a successful download. Both are useless.

**So the last step of every fetch is to open the file and look.** If the plan names and prices are there, the clipping worked. If the file is 40 words of apology, that page needs a different route, which chapter 7 covers.

Tomas set his agent to fetch 4 rivals' changelogs every night and did not look for two weeks. On day 15 he opened the folder: 56 neat dated files, each 38 words long, each saying 'Checking your browser before you continue.' Spot it fast: a file far smaller than the page looks on screen, or **the same size every single day**.

cards.prompt: When the agent 'fetches and keeps a copy', which of these is the clipping clerk actually doing?

options.text: Reading today's paper carefully and remembering the main points
Buying today's paper, stripping it to plain words, filing it under today's date
Cutting out only the stories that changed since yesterday

whyNot.a: That's the model's job in chapter 5, and memory isn't a file: the agent keeps nothing between runs unless you save it.
whyNot.c: That's the scissors, chapter 4: you cannot cut what changed until you own two dated copies.

cards.reteach: Fetching is the dull step: get the text, drop the tags, save with the date. Comparing and explaining come later and lean on it. No copy, no diff; no diff, no summary.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
The agent downloads a page as raw text, strips the tags down to the words a person sees, and saves the result in a file named with today's date; then you open it to check it is not an 'enable JavaScript' shell. **Yesterday's file is the only reason today's can mean anything.**

Tomorrow: the scissors. Two dated copies, and only the lines that differ.

Open one rival's pricing page, select all, copy, and paste into a new text note. Name it with the company and today's date, like lantern-pricing-2026-10-04. You just did the agent's job by hand, once.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now fetch one competitor page, save its text under today's date, and open it to prove the copy is real.
